problem: A comic plea or complaint chorus stays at one politeness level and the payoff never lands.
technique: Order the chorus from politest to bluntest: open on the courteous ask (the title), add one small, petty, checkable stake, then a line that ranks two kinds of hurt with the pettier one winning, and end on the bluntest word the narrator would really say. The title stays sweet and repeatable; the edge sits at the end of the chorus.
example: In Please Please Please the tripled polite request opens the chorus, a comic stake about having just done her makeup follows, then a line ranking heartbreak below ego, and the chorus closes on a profane word Carpenter says arrived as an ad lib with the melody pushed lower.
limits: Line order is lexical, seen through tool paraphrase of a press print, not an official lyric; the low-note and ad-lib claims are writer statements, not checked by listening.
when_not: A sincere ballad or a grief song, where the blunt last word reads as aggression and ranking vanity above loss trivialises it; and repeated across a whole album it becomes the shtick critics punished on Man's Best Friend (AA-S21).
distinct_from: C05 (sincere line then joke): a two-line pairing, usually in a bridge; this is the order of a whole chorus, polite to blunt
C14 (blunt fact undercut by dry humour): this card saves the bluntness for the end instead of leading with it
C03 (keep the flinch line): that decides whether to keep a risky word; this decides where it goes

problem: A where-I'm-from or outsider song: naming the hometown makes it small, naming nothing makes it vague.
technique: Put the famous place the song rejects in the title, as a negation, and leave the affirmed place unnamed so each listener supplies their own; anchor the blank with one concrete third-person portrait in verse 1. Decide on purpose whether to fill the blank: leave it open for participation, or name one real place for specificity.
example: In Ain't In LA the only place named in the lyric is Los Angeles, and only to deny it; verse 1 is a girl's bedroom, clothes and posters somewhere unnamed. Listeners posted videos of their own hometowns, while critics wanted Bratislava named.
limits: Lexical, via tool paraphrase of a press print; the listener response is press-reported; no writer says the blank was deliberate.
when_not: When the song honours one real town, naming it is stronger; and without a concrete portrait in the verses the blank reads as generic (Kuppermann, Doyle in AD-S36).
distinct_from: C41 (place as value system, refusal, one person then a crowd; advises naming at least one place): this card isolates the negated title and treats naming versus leaving blank as a choice with a cost either way
C23 (unnamed addressee anchored in one image): that is about a person; this is about a place in the title

problem: A verse where the narrator drifts into a fantasy sits at the same level as the rest, and the return to the chorus does not feel like waking up.
technique: Set the daydream section apart from the rest of the song so it sounds suspended (Antonoff moved the second verse from A up to C, a modulation he describes as unnatural), and let the return to the home key for the chorus snap the narrator back. In the words, end the fantasy with a joking retraction that leaves the wish standing.
example: In Please Please Please verse 2 imagines a hidden, stay-at-home version of the relationship and then calls it a joke; Antonoff says the chord shift puts it somewhere dreamlike and the return to A pops the bubble.
limits: Musical claim from a writer statement in a tool-extracted transcript, corroborated only by press noting a key change on verse 2; the key sequence afterwards is ambiguous; not checked by listening.
when_not: When the section is not a departure from the song's reality the shift is a gimmick; and a retraction that arrives too fast kills the wish before it registers.
distinct_from: C21 (try a key change before rewriting a flat chorus): there the key change is a fix for lift; here it marks a fantasy and its end
C50 (lift the last chorus with harmony or register): this is a mid-song departure and return, not a final lift
